name: In-office professional bleaching

lead: In-office bleaching is tooth whitening done by a dentist or hygienist with a high-strength peroxide gel. It is the fastest route to lighter teeth, and the shade change shows after a single visit.

Hydrogen peroxide, or carbamide peroxide that releases it, makes free radicals that break down pigment inside the tooth so less light is absorbed. Wikipedia describes shade improvements of roughly 2 to 7 shades with effects lasting months, and says nearly half the change from a one-hour session may be lost within a week as teeth rehydrate.

paras: The dentist cleans the teeth, protects the gums with a barrier, applies the gel and sometimes uses a light, over about an hour. Many people repeat treatments or follow with take-home trays to keep the shade; a 2015 study cited by Wikipedia found no added benefit from the light.

Reported tooth sensitivity ranged from 67 to 78 percent in cited in-office studies, lasting roughly 4 to 39 days. Peroxide at 10 percent or more can irritate gums, and bonded restorations can be affected. Listed contraindications include pregnancy, breastfeeding, age under 16, untreated decay or gum disease and exposed dentine. In the EU, higher-strength products are limited to dental professionals.

chain: Visibly whiter teeth in one visit
angle.text: In-office bleaching is the fastest way to whiten: a dentist applies strong peroxide gel and the shade change shows after one visit. Colour fades over months and sensitivity is common, so some people repeat it.

lead: In-office professional bleaching is tooth whitening carried out by a dentist or hygienist using a high-concentration peroxide gel, in a single visit that visibly lightens teeth for a brighter, more polished smile. The active agents are hydrogen peroxide and carbamide peroxide, which releases hydrogen peroxide on contact with water; the peroxide produces free radicals that break down pigment molecules so teeth reflect less light [1].

A typical in-office visit begins with an examination and cleaning, with the gums covered by a light-cured barrier. Wikipedia reports gels with 10 to 44 percent carbamide peroxide (about 3 to 16 percent hydrogen peroxide), and power bleaching with 25 to 38 percent hydrogen peroxide for 6 to 15 minutes of light exposure [1]. Branded systems are named in forum discussion, such as Zoom and Opalescence Boost.

Cited sources describe shade improvement of 2 to 7 shades, with colour that can fade and a partial early rebound; sensitivity is common [1]. Systematic reviews of in-office bleaching examine gel concentration and ways to reduce sensitivity [2][2].

paras: According to Wikipedia, the dentist examines and cleans the teeth, protects the gums, and applies the gel, sometimes with a light source such as halogen, LED or plasma arc lamps, most in the blue spectrum [1]. Internal bleaching is a separate approach for root-canal-treated teeth and carries a risk of root resorption [1].

Wikipedia says light can enhance whitening without added sensitivity when used properly, but cites a 2015 study in which light activation did not improve results and likely raised tissue temperature [1].

Wikipedia describes in-office whitening as faster and more effective than take-home options, though that statement is tagged as needing medical citation [1]. Bleaching is described as working best on yellow teeth and least on grayish ones, with uneven results common [1].

Nearly half the colour change from a one-hour session may be lost within seven days, linked to dehydration of the tooth, and stains can return within months; retreatment every six to twelve months is mentioned [1].

Cited figures show 67 to 78 percent of in-office patients reporting sensitivity where hydrogen peroxide and heat were used, lasting roughly 4 to 39 days; potassium nitrate and fluoride toothpastes ease discomfort [1]. Hydrogen peroxide at 10 percent or more can damage tissue, and chemical burns often follow poorly fitting trays [1].

Other reported effects include increased enamel roughness and porosity, reduced composite bond strength, and temporary mercury release from amalgam [1]. The IARC found insufficient evidence that hydrogen peroxide is a human carcinogen [1]. Contraindications listed include age under 16, pregnancy or breastfeeding, untreated gum disease or decay, cracks or exposed dentine, and peroxide allergy [1].

Reviews of randomized trials report that higher peroxide concentrations cause more sensitivity [2]. Desensitizing toothpastes reduced sensitivity in some in-office regimens but not others [2]. Wikipedia notes potassium nitrate and fluoride toothpastes ease discomfort [1].

In-office bleaching is discussed in appearance communities as a fast route to lighter teeth compared with take-home gels, and branded systems such as Zoom and Opalescence Boost are named in forum discussion [1]. Practitioners and users often pair it with photos or events because the result appears within one visit, although part of the early change can rebound within a week [1].

In the EU, retail products are limited to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide, and up to 6 percent may only be provided by a certified dental professional to patients aged 18 or older [1]. The US FDA is cited as endorsing gels under 6 percent hydrogen peroxide or up to 16 percent carbamide peroxide for consumer products [1].

A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis in Operative Dentistry covered 14 studies (7 in the meta-analysis, 649 patients, follow-up one week to 12 months) comparing bleaching gel concentrations. It found higher sensitivity with high-concentration hydrogen peroxide, a significant difference in objective colour change (delta E), and no significant difference in subjective colour change [2].

A 2024 systematic review in Clinical Oral Investigations of five randomized trials (387 people) found desensitizing toothpastes effectively reduced sensitivity after single-session in-office bleaching with 35% hydrogen peroxide and after home bleaching with 22% carbamide peroxide, but not after two-session in-office bleaching with 35% or 38% hydrogen peroxide or home bleaching with 16% carbamide peroxide [2]. Wikipedia also summarises research on bleaching generally [1].
